title: Cc No. 715/Pn/10 Sh. Chirag Sahni vs . Sh. Yogender Singh Page No. 1 Of 13 on 7 May, 2015
full_text: Cc No. 715/Pn/10 Sh. Chirag Sahni vs . Sh. Yogender Singh Page No. 1 Of 13 on 7 May, 2015 IN THE COURT OF MS. RIYA GUHA, METROPOLITIAN MAGISTRATE (NI Act -02), CENTRAL, TIS HAZARI COURT, DELHI CC No. 715/PN/10 UID NO. 02401R0557862010 Sh. Chirag Sahni S/o Late Sh. Varun Sahni R/o 6/16, West Patel Nagar New Delhi-110 008 .......Complainant Versus Sh. Yogender Singh S/o Sh. Bhajan Singh 2116/2A, Gali No. 6, Prem Nagar, New Delhi Also at: E-4 & E-5, Sewak Park Uttam Nagar, New Delhi-110 059 ...........Accused The offence complained of : u/s 138 NI Act The plea of the accused person : Not guilty Final order : conviction Date of institution of complaint : 06.12.2010 Date on which reserved for judgment : 27.04.2015 Date of pronouncement of judgment : 07.05.2015 JUDGMENT: 1. Vide this judgment, the Court shall decide the liability of the accused persons in the present case filed under Section 138 of N.I. Act. The brief facts of the case necessary for the disposal of the present matter are laid down below: CC No. 715/PN/10 Sh. Chirag Sahni vs. Sh. Yogender Singh Page no. 1 of 13 2. It is the case of the complainant that he is engaged in the business of properties and the accused is his family friend and that he had approached the complainant for the loan of Rs. 2,50,000/- in January 2003 on the condition that he will pay back the loan within one year. Accordingly, acceding to the request of the accused, the complainant had given the loan of Rs. 2,50,000/- to him in January 2003 to be repaid within a period of one year along with interest @24% per annum. 3. It is further submitted that the accused did not pay the above mentioned loan amount after completion of the loan term and after intervention of family and friends, a settlement agreement had been executed between the complainant and the accused for the settlement of the above said loan dispute for lumpsum amount of Rs. 5 lakhs including the interest upto June 2007. As per the settlement agreement dated 13/06/2007, the accused had promised the complainant to make the said payment on or before 30.06.2008 but even after expiration of the date of the payment, the accused had not made the payment and demanded some more time to make such payment. Further, the accused had issued a promissory note of Rs. 5 lakhs in favour of the complainant wherein the accused had promised to make the payment on or before 31/12/2009. The original settlement agreement dated 13.06.2007 is Ex. CW1/A and the original promissory note is Ex. CW1/B. 4. It is submitted that as per the settlement agreement and promissory note, the accused had issued cheque bearing no. 290572 dated 03/09/2010 drawn fro m HDFC Bank, K.G. Marg, New Delhi for sum of Rs. 5 lakhs in favour of the complainant and assured that the said cheque will be honoured positively on its presentation. The original cheque bearing no. 290572 dated 03/09/2010 of Rs. 5 lakhs is Ex. CW1/C. CC No. 715/PN/10 Sh. Chirag Sahni vs. Sh. Yogender Singh Page no. 2 of 13 5. It is further submitted by the complainant that the said cheque was presented by him with his banker for its encashment but the cheques returned dishonoured with the remarks 'insufficient funds' vide return memo dated 04/09/2010. It is further submitted by the complainant that his client had again contacted the accused and he told the complainant to present the cheque after one month. The complainant had again presented the cheque for encashment but the same was returned unpaid by the banker with the reason 'insufficient funds' vide cheque return memo dated 18/10/2010. The cheque returning memos are Ex.CW1/D and Ex.CW1/E. Thereafter, the complainant got issued a legal demand notice dated 29/10/2010 through his counsel, which was sent by Speed Post and UPC. The copy of the legal demand notice is Ex.CW1/F and the speed post and the UPC receipts are Ex.CW1/G1 and Ex.CW1/G2 respectively. Despite the service of the legal demand notice and despite expiry of the statutory period, the accused had failed to pay the cheque amount to the complainant, hence the complainant had filed the present complaint case. 6. Thereafter, after due consideration, the Ld. Predecessor Court had passed the summoning order dated 14/12/2010 issuing summons to the accused. The accused had appeared and was duly admitted on bail. Notice against the the accused under Section 251 Cr. PC was framed on 13.08.2013. In his plea of defence, the accused Yogender Singh submitted that: "I do not plead guilty and claim trial. In fact, the complainant received the cheque and obtained my signatures on so many documents as I have borrowed Rs. 10,000/- from the complainant and after three months, I had paid Rs. 12,000/- to the complainant and so many times, I made a request to the complainant to get back my cheques and documents but he always took one pretext or the other and in the year 2008 I had changed my residence from 2116/2 A-1, Gali No. 6, Prem Nagar to E-5, Sewak Park, Uttam Nagar, Delhi-59. Thereafter, I forget these documents and cheque due to lapse of time and the complainant uses all these documents against me in the present case just to harass me and it is a false case. It is also important CC No. 715/PN/10 Sh. Chirag Sahni vs. Sh. Yogender Singh Page no. 3 of 13 to mention here that all the handwriting appears on the documents are not of mine except my signatures which were used against me by the complainant dishonestly". 7. Thereafter, the matter was posted for defence evidence and the accused produced one witness namely Mr. Kanhiya whose testimony was recorded as DW1. The DW1 was duly cross-examined by the Ld.Counsel of the complainant. The DW1 Mr.Kanhaiya deposed that he had known the accused since long and the name of the father of the accused is Sh.Bhajan Singh and that he resides in Sewa Park, Delhi. He further stated that he alongwith the accused went to the complainant house and the accused received Rs.10,000/- from the complainant, and that the accused handed over a blank signed cheque to the complainant. Further deposed that the complainant demanded back the money so the accused returned Rs.12,000/- with 4% interest in cash to the complainant. The DW1 further deposed that the cheque was not returned by the complainant. 8. The DW1 was duly cross-examined by the Ld. Counsel of the complainant. Thereafter, the accused Yogender Singh stepped into the witness box to depose in his own behalf. His testimony was recorded as DW2 and he was duly cross-examined by the Ld.Counsel of the complainant. In his defence, the accused has submitted that he had taken Rs. 10,000/- from the complainant and the complainant demanded security cheque and some documents in lieu of giving such amount of Rs. 10,000/-. He further submitted that he had handed over Rs. 12,000/- in cash to the complainant in the month of April along with interest. Thereafter, he had asked to return the security cheque as well as the documents which he had handed over to the complainant. It is further stated by the accused that he had shifted to Dwarka and he had asked the complainant to return the said cheque along with the documents but the complainant did not return the same and the complainant CC No. 715/PN/10 Sh. Chirag Sahni vs. Sh. Yogender Singh Page no. 4 of 13 has filed a false case against him 9. Thereafter, on closure of evidence, the matter was posted for final arguments which had had been advanced by both the parties. To bring out an offence under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, the complainant must successfully prove all the essential requirements as laid down in that provision i.e. : a) The cheque for an amount is issue by the accused to the complainant on a bank accountmaintained by him. b) The said cheque is issued for the discharge, in whole or in part of any debt or other liability by the acused. c) The cheque is returned by the bank unpaid on account of insufficient amount to honour the cheque. d) The cheque is presented to the bank within 6 months from the date on which it is drawn and is within the period of its validity. e) Within 30 days demand notice is issued by the complainant on receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the dishonour of the cheque. f) The drawer of the said cheque / accused fails to make the payment of the said amount of the money to the complainant within 15 days of the said notice. g) The debt or liability against which the cheque was issued is legally enforceable. 10. In order to have the positive outcome in his favour, the complainant was required to show that the cheque Ex. CW1/C was given by the accused to discharge his liabilities which was dishonoured via returning memo whereafter the accused had also failed to comply with the requirements of the legal notice Ex. CW1/F. On the other hand, the accused was required to show his defence in the balance of preponderance of probabilities that the cheque was not issued for any legally enforceable liability or that no offence under Section 138 of N.I. Act is made out against him. 11. As per section 118 NI Act, it is to be presumed in favour of the complainant during the trial that the cheque in question was given against consideration by the accused and that the complainant was the holder of the said cheque in due course. Further as per Sec. 139 NI Act, it is to be presumed in favour of the complainant during the trial that the cheque in question was CC No. 715/PN/10 Sh. Chirag Sahni vs. Sh. Yogender Singh Page no. 5 of 13 received by the complainant against a debt or liability. Reliance can be placed on "Rangappa Vs. Sri Mohan" SLP (Crl.) 407/06, Dated:- 07.05.2010. 12. It is well settled that both the aforesaid presumptions U/s 118 and 139 of NI Act are rebuttable in nature and the onus to rebut the same squarely rests upon the accused. The accused can rebut these presumptions not merely by examining his own witnesses but also through the cross examination of the complainant and his witnesses thereby bringing on record through the entire evidence available on record, that the complainant case is false and that there was no existing liabilities between the parties and that the cheque in question was misused. The accused has a right to argue his case even on the basis of the cross examination of the complainant and his witnesses to show to the court that there existed no legally recoverable debt or liability between the parties. In order to rebut the legal presumption in question, it emerges that the accused need not require direct evidence to disprove the existence of consideration. If the accused succeeds in raising a probable defence by referring to his own evidence (if any) and from the evidence of the complainant, then the onus would shift on to the complainant, who then would have to show beyond reasonable doubt the existence of consideration/existence of a legally recoverable debt or liability in respect of the cheque in question. 13. The defence set up by the accused in the present case is that the cheque was issued in blank as a security of loan of only Rs.10,000/- taken from the complainant which the accused has already returned alongwith interest. It is also the defence of the accused that he had also asked for return of the cheque and the documents from the complainant but the complainant had not returned the cheque but misused the same by presenting it and the by filing the present case. CC No. 715/PN/10 Sh. Chirag Sahni vs. Sh. Yogender Singh Page no. 6 of 13 14. It is argued by the Ld. counsel for complainant that from evidence on record, the complainant has proved that cheque in question was signed by the accused which was dishonoured vide memo and despite the legal notice accused did not make the payment. It is further argued that the entire case of the complainant has remained unrebutted and that accused has failed to discharge the burden upon him to rebutt the presumption in favour of the complainant under the Act. The accused, on the other hand, has argued that he is having no legal liability towards the complainant because the cheque in question was given in blank only in lieu of loan taken which already stands repaid. 15. The accused may adduce direct evidence on preponderance of probabilities to prove that cheque in question was not supported by any consideration and that there was no debt or liability to be discharged by him. However, there is no need that the accused should disprove the non existence of consideration and debt by leading direct evidence because the existence of negative evidence is neither possible nor contemplated. At the same time it is clear that bare denial of the passing of the consideration and existence of debt, apparently would not serve the purpose of the accused. Something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the burden of proof shifted to the complainant. 16. The question which becomes important in this scenario is that whether the complainant proved his case, that whether the amount was legally enforceable debt. The offence under Section 138 of the Act is a technical offence and the complainant is only supposed to prove that the cheque issued by the accused was dishonoured, his statement that cheque was issued against liability or debt is sufficient proof of the debt or liability and the onus shifts to the accused to show the circumstances under which the cheque was CC No. 715/PN/10 Sh. Chirag Sahni vs. Sh. Yogender Singh Page no. 7 of 13 issued and this could be proved by the accused only by way of cogent evidence. 17. The issuance of the cheque is not disputed by the accused. It is further established on record that the cheque in question issued by the accused got dishonored vide bank memos twice. The signatures on the cheque in question is not disputed by the accused at all. It is also established on record that the cheque in question pertains to the account of the accused. 18. During recording of his statement under section 313 CrPC, the accused had stated that the cheque had been given by him as blank as a security and has been manipulated and falsely presented is of no consequence. The Court is of the considered view that a bare explanation of accused cannot be accepted in the absence of any supporting material. In V S Yadav vs Reena CrLA No. 1136/2010 decided on 21.09.2010, Hon'ble High Court of Delhi has observed that: "Mere pleading not guilty and stating that the cheques were issued as security, would not give amount to rebutting the presumption raised under Section 139 of N.I. Act." ......................... "If no loan was given, but cheques were retained, he immediately would have protested and asked the cheques to be returned and if still cheques were not returned, he would have served a notice as complainant. Nothing was proved in this case." 19. So far as the defence that other columns in cheque were not filled in by the accused is concerned, this contention does not have any force. No law requires that all the columns must be filled in by the drawer/maker himself. If signature on the cheque is admitted, the same will be sufficient. The concept of blank signed cheque is virtually immaterial in view of several judgments of Hon'ble High Court of Delhi viz. " Ravi Chopra vs State And Anr. "2008(2) JCC (NI) 169, "Vijender Singh vs M/s EICHER MOTORS Ltd & ANR." CRL. CC No. 715/PN/10 Sh. Chirag Sahni vs. Sh. Yogender Singh Page no. 8 of 13 M.C. No. 1454/2011 decided on 05.05.2011," Tarun Gautam vs State" Crl M C No.529/2012 decided on 13.02.2012 and "Manoj Sharma vs Anil Aggarwal" CRL.M.C. 1325/2012 decided on 20.04.2012. 20. The accused has not denied the signatures on the cheque in question. Therefore, mere pleading not guilty and stating that the loan amount has been returned, would not amount to rebutting the presumption raised under Section 139 of N.I Act. In the present case accused has not produced any cogent proof in support of his any defence that the cheque in question given in blank as security to the complainant which makes it improbable that the cheque in question was not issued towards the discharge of legal liability as alleged by the complainant. 21. In this case the accused had not sought any permission of the court to cross-examine the complainant. As per the judgment of " Rajesh Agarwal versus State and Anr " III(2010)DLT(Crl)349, which prescribed the procedure to be followed in complaint cases filed under section 138 of the NI Act, it has been categorically held that a complainant is to be recalled and re-examined only if an application under section 145(2) of the Act is moved by the accused at the appropriate stage, and disclosing the specific reasons along with his defence as to why he wants to recall the complainant for his cross- examination. In this case the accused had not moved any such application seeking cross-examination of the complainant, hence as far as the complainant's case is concerned the same remains unrebutted. Accordingly, the argument of the Ld. Counsel of the accused that the complainant did not produce a single witness of the loan transaction or of the documents, is unacceptable and deserves to be dismissed, as the evidence of the complainant given during the presummoning stage is sufficient to proceed with the trial, especially in view of Section 118 and 139 of the NI Act. CC No. 715/PN/10 Sh. Chirag Sahni vs. Sh. Yogender Singh Page no. 9 of 13 22. Furthermore, the accused has denied that the legal notice has been received by him. In this regard, the complainant has placed on record the copy of the legal notice Ex.CW1/F alongwith postal receipts Ex.CW1/G1 and UPC receiot Ex. CW1/2 . It is a settled position of law that a notice properly addressed, prepaid and posted by registered post shall be deemed to be served upon the respondent unless the contrary is proved. In such scenario, the decision of Hon'ble Supreme Court in " Alavi Hazi v. Palapetty Muhammad & Anr. " 2007 STPL (DC) 952 SC would become applicable wherein Hon'ble Apex Court has held that even if the accused did not receive the legal demand notice he can pay the cheque amount within fifteen days of the service of summons from the court but if he fails, he cannot contend that he has not received the legal demand notice. It is evident that the drawer has failed to make the payment of cheque amount in question within 15 days of the receipt of aforesaid notice, thus, the present complaint U/s 138 NI Act has been initiated against the accused. Morever, the presumption of deemed service of legal demand notice becomes operative as there is mere denial without any proof shown by the accused, and also because the address submiited by the accused in his bail-bonds is the same in which the legal demand notice had been sent. 23. During the cross-examination of the DW1 Mr.Kanhaiya he stated that he alongwith the accused went to the house of the complainant about 4/5 years ago but he could not remember the exact date. He further deposed that he did not remember the address of the complainant. He stated that he did not know the name of the bank of which the cheque was given and the cheque number given to the complainant. He further deposed that he met with the complainant two times at the time of receiving of Rs. 10,000/- and at the time of giving of Rs. 12,000/-, he do not know the date of payment of Rs. 12,000/-. He further stated that no receipt of payment of Rs. 12000/- was taken by the accused he CC No. 715/PN/10 Sh. Chirag Sahni vs. Sh. Yogender Singh Page no. 10 of 13 denied the suggestion that the accused has not made the payment of Rs. 12,000/- . Further, the DW1 stated that as Rs. 5 lacs was not given in his presence hence, he did not know whether the accused had given any promissory note of such amount or signed any agreement/undertaking for the payment of such amount of Rs. 5 lacs to the complainant. Hence, the testimony of this DW was shaken when put to cross-examination. Further, he is not a witness to the loan transaction nor was he present when the loan was advanced or the Ex.CW1/A or Ex.CW1/B was executed. It is clear that the DW1 was an interested witness who deposed at the instance of the accused. 24. When the accued was cross-examined by the Ld. Counsel for the complainant, he reiterated his defence that he had taken a loan of Rs. 10,000/- from the complainant in the year 2008 and denied that he had taken a loan of Rs. 2.5 Lacs from the complainant in the year 2003. He further affirmed the suggestion that settlement exhibited as Ex. CW1/A and the promissory note Ex. CW1/B bore his signatures and thumb impression. The Ld. Counsel for the accused has argued that the documents were obtained by the complainant with only signatures of the accused and the Ex. CW1/A and Ex. CW1/B are manipulated. However, it is well-established from the cross-examination of the accused that he was an educated and literate person and working in a official capacity in a business concern. It is improbable that a person who is educated and literate as well, will give his signatures on any blank document. 25. Perusal of the Ex. CW1/A and the Ex. CW1/B shows that the accused put his signatures in English. Hence, it is clear that the accused is also aware of the English language. Again, it becomes difficult to believe that a working and salaried person will put his signatures and thumb impressions on a bare and blank documents. Hence, the accused has been unable to prove that his signatures and thumb impressions were obtained by the complainant on blank CC No. 715/PN/10 Sh. Chirag Sahni vs. Sh. Yogender Singh Page no. 11 of 13 documents. 26. The accused was also cross-examined on the aspect of his version that he has repaid an amount of Rs. 12,000/- to the complainant. However, the accused was unable to state the exact date when he had returned such alleged loan amount to the complainant. He also admitted that he has no receipt of payment of Rs. 12,000/- from the complainant. In the considered view of the Court, such response must result in drawing an adverse inference against the accused as it cannot be believed that a person who has issued a blank signed cheque in favour of another will not insist for its return when he has repaid the loan amount and wlii not even ask for a receipt of the alleged repayment. 27. It is also evident that the accused did not take any action against the complainant, by way of sending a letter or notice, for return of the cheque. These circumstances throws a doubt on his version as it cannot be believed that a person will neither take any receipts for repayment of loan nor will he strive to ask for return of the cheque when he has repaid the loan. The accused had only taken a vague plea that the complainant did not return the cheque despite assurance. In the judgment " K.N. Beena Vs. Muniyappan , AIR 2001 SC 2895", it was held that mere denial / averments in reply by the accused are not sufficient to shift the burden of proof onto the complainant. Accused has to prove in trial by leading cogent evidence that there was no debt or liability, which in the present case accused has not been done. 28. Reading of the evidence on record in its entirety, would show that the evidence is not supportive with the innocence of the accused and proves the case of the complainant beyond reasonable doubts. Secondly, accused has not produced any cogent proof in support of his defence on record. The CC No. 715/PN/10 Sh. Chirag Sahni vs. Sh. Yogender Singh Page no. 12 of 13 accused has failed to discharge the onus. Hence, this court holds that the accused has not been able to rebut the presumptions under section 139 and 118 NI Act standing in favour of complainant. 29. Having considered the entire evidence, the complainant successfully proved all the essential requirements of Section 138 of the Act. Accordingly, accused Sh. Yogender Singh, S/o Sh. Bhajan Singh is held guilty for committing the offence punishable u/s 138 of the Act, he is hereby convicted for the said offence. 30. Let he be heard on point of sentence separately on 14/05/2015. Pronounced in the open (RIYA GUHA) court on 07/05/2015 MM (C-02)/Delhi CC No. 715/PN/10 Sh. Chirag Sahni vs. Sh. Yogender Singh Page no. 13 of 13
